blind_rationale:
Lewis (2014) evaluates two pilot output-based intergovernmental performance grants in Indonesia: P2D2 (DAK Reimbursement, 2011–12, N = 218 pooled kabupaten/kota-year observations across 67 PSM-matched pairs) and Water Hibah (WH, 2010–11, N = 105 pooled kabupaten/kota-year observations across 34 PSM-matched pairs). Only the Water Hibah analysis measures a Criterion 4 household water access outcome—log of new operational PDAM household piped water connections per 1,000 people (Tables 8–10; P2D2 measures aggregate local capital spending across all sectors because water/sanitation spending could not be disaggregated, Footnote 5, p. 418, and WH Tables 5–7 measure an institutional/fiscal intermediate outcome, local government equity investment in PDAMs).

On Criterion 2, Water Hibah is a borderline fiscal-governance exposure (`borderline_governance_or_proxy`) warranting PI scope scrutiny against `E03` (financial/capital subsidy without a household-facing legal rule): WH is an AusAID-backed Ministry of Finance output-based intergovernmental grant rule requiring local governments to make upfront matching equity investments in their municipal water utilities (PDAMs) and disbursing Rp 2–3 million per independently verified operational connection (~45% of connection cost). While this embodies formal intergovernmental conditional-transfer and verification rules, its mechanism is fundamentally a capital-financing subsidy, and Footnote 6 notes data do not allow testing whether connections actually reached poor households (the stated pro-poor targeting rule).

Classifying S636 as `none_nonfit` (outside SWiM Families A, B, and C) is strongly justified on both substantive and econometric grounds:
1. Over-control for the causal mediator in all binary-program connection models: By program design, WH increases household connections *by inducing local government equity investment in PDAMs* (Table 7: +739.1 constant-2000 Rp/capita, z = 3.20). However, Lewis never estimates the total (reduced-form) effect of WH participation on household connections. Every connection model (Tables 8–10) includes PDAM equity investment per capita alongside the WH dummy, leaving only the mediator-blocked direct effect of WH participation holding investment fixed—which is statistically non-significant in the author's preferred endogenous specifications (Table 8: beta = 0.3816, t = 1.58; Table 10: beta = 0.2892, t = 1.04). Moreover, the IV endogenous specification uses on/off-Java location and year dummies as excluded instruments for transfers/investment, which plausibly violate the exclusion restriction for water connection growth.
2. Continuous fiscal-expenditure scaling: The statistically significant predictors in Tables 8 and 10 (`Investment per capita` beta = 0.0002, t = 2.30; `Hibah financed investments per capita` beta = 0.0004, t = 1.71) are capital-spending semi-elasticities per constant-2000 Rupiah per capita rather than legal/institutional rule effects. If a total binary WH program estimate were nevertheless forced into a SWiM family, its closest substantive neighbours would be Family B (conditional external financial/grant support) or Family C (intergovernmental administrative performance-contracting incentives), but `none_nonfit` is more rigorous given the fiscal-subsidy mechanism and mediator-adjusted specification.

headline_estimate_summary:
Water Hibah (WH) household piped water connections models (Outcome: log of number of new household water connections per 1,000 people; N = 105 pooled kabupaten/kota-year observations across 2010–11; covariates: log population, % urban, % poor, lagged % population with access to water, log GRDP per capita; fiscal inputs in constant-2000 Rp per capita; robust/bootstrapped t-statistics; SEs and CIs not printed):
- Table 8 (PDF p. 15 / p. 428), Preferred Endogenous-Investment IV Model (R2 = 0.413): WH program participation dummy beta = 0.3816 (t = 1.58, ns, implied SE = 0.2415; positive sign = more new household connections, but conditioned on predicted PDAM equity investment); Predicted PDAM equity investment per capita beta = 0.0002 (t = 2.30, p < 0.05; implied unit cost = Rp 4.3M/connection in 2010–11 prices). Exogenous OLS comparison (R2 = 0.472): WH dummy beta = 0.4915 (t = 2.77, p < 0.05, implied SE = 0.1774); Investment per capita beta = 0.0001 (t = 4.07, p < 0.05; implied unit cost = Rp 6.3M/connection).
- Table 9 (PDF p. 15 / p. 428, interaction test, N = 105): Endogenous model WH dummy beta = 0.5523 (t = 1.90, printed with ** though two-sided p ~ 0.06), Investments per capita beta = 0.0005 (t = 1.75, p < 0.10), WH dummy x investments per capita beta = -0.0002 (t = -0.99, ns; exogenous interaction beta = 0.0000, t = 0.15, ns).
- Table 10 (PDF p. 17 / p. 430, disaggregating funding source, N = 105; note table footnote mislabels DV as equity investment): Endogenous model Treatment dummy beta = 0.2892 (t = 1.04, ns), Hibah-financed investments per capita beta = 0.0004 (t = 1.71, p < 0.10; Rp 2.5M/connection), Other revenue-financed investments per capita beta = 0.0001 (t = 1.69, p < 0.10; Rp 6.9M/connection). Exogenous model: Treatment dummy beta = 0.3034 (t = 1.62, ns), Hibah-financed investments per capita beta = 0.0003 (t = 6.16, p < 0.05; Rp 2.9M/connection), Other revenue-financed investments per capita beta = 0.0001 (t = 3.42, p < 0.05; Rp 8.2M/connection).
- Intermediate & non-water outcomes: WH hurdle model for per-capita PDAM equity investment (Table 7, PDF p. 14 / p. 427, N = 105/73) yields WH dummy = +739.1 constant-2000 Rp/capita or Rp 2,141 in 2010–11 prices (z = 3.20, p < 0.05, endogenous) and Hibah per capita = 0.815 (z = 2.50, p < 0.05). P2D2 aggregate all-sector capital spending (Tables 3–4, PDF pp. 10, 12, N = 218) yields P2D2 dummy = -0.058 (t = -0.86, ns) alone, and P2D2 x log DAK per capita = +0.216 (t = 2.43, p < 0.05).
study_design_and_sample: Quasi-experimental ("doubly robust") propensity score matching (1:1 nearest-neighbour without replacement) combined with pooled cross-sectional OLS, two-part hurdle, and instrumental-variables (bootstrapped SE) regressions in Indonesia, using local governments (kabupaten and kota) and their municipal water utilities (PDAMs) as the unit of analysis. Two pilot programs are analysed: (1) Water Hibah (2010–11): 35 treatment local governments matched on 2008–09 baseline covariates to 35 control local governments (from 65 slated for 2013 entry), with 1 treatment unit dropped off common support = 34 treatment and 34 control local governments, yielding N = 105 pooled local government-year observations (N = 73 positive-investment observations in Table 6 hurdle stage 2); and (2) P2D2 / DAK Reimbursement (2011–12, all-sector capital spending): two-stage PSM matching 5 treatment to 5 control provinces and 68 treatment to 68 control local governments (1 dropped off common support = 67 matched pairs), yielding N = 218 pooled local government-year observations in regressions (Tables 3–4).
